entry.title: My city. My problem. My solution: Nairobi through curious eyes | ZEISS

media:group.media:title: My city. My problem. My solution: Nairobi through curious eyes | ZEISS
media:group.media:description:
Through the Nairobi Youth Innovation Challenge, students from schools across Nairobi used ZEISS microscopes to investigate local challenges and develop ideas for their communities. Supported by teachers and mentors from the University of Nairobi, they experienced firsthand how science can help address real-life problems.
Throughout the project, students documented their progress using vivo smartphones. Much of the footage featured in this video was captured by the participants themselves.
The challenge is part of “A Heart for Science,” a global ZEISS initiative that encourages young people to explore STEM through hands-on learning.
__________
What is A Heart for Science? 🔬🧒👦👧
Enthusiasm for nature and technology has always been an integral part of ZEISS' DNA. On the occasion of the company's 175th anniversary, ZEISS launched “A Heart for Science” – an international initiative run by ZEISS that aims to get young people under 18 interested in STEM. What is special about it is that any of our employees can impart their knowledge to the explorers of tomorrow.
More information about the initiative: https://zeiss.ly/AHfS

media:group.media:title: Photonics powers AI | ZEISS
media:group.media:description:
What if the future of AI runs on light?⚡
Photonics is making AI faster, more powerful – and more energy-efficient.
This is where Photonic Integrated Circuits (PICs) come in.
Rather than moving information with electrical signals, Photonic Integrated Circuits use light – enabling much faster and more energy-efficient data processing.
As demand for speed and efficiency grows, PICs are becoming essential for AI, data centers, and next-generation technologies.
Smaller, faster, more efficient: that’s the power of light.

media:group.media:title: Inspiring curiosity through microscopy | ZEISS
media:group.media:description:
How do you inspire curiosity for science? Sometimes, all it takes is a closer look.
Our senses are remarkable, but they have their limits. Optical tools like microscopes help reveal details that remain invisible to the naked eye and open up entirely new perspectives on the world around us.
Through hands-on microscopy experiences, students can explore, ask questions, make discoveries, and experience what it feels like to think and work like scientists. These early encounters with science help foster curiosity, creative thinking, problem-solving skills, and an interest in STEM subjects.
Through the ZEISS Promotion Fund, ZEISS supports STEM education and long-term partnerships with regional educational initiatives, helping young people discover the fascination of science and technology.

media:group.media:title: How does fluorescence work? | ZEISS
media:group.media:description:
Magical blue glowing waves at night. 🌊 That’s not magic, that’s fluorescence.
Fluorescent microscopes use the same trick: • Scientists can highlight specific structures inside the cell. • The microscope shines light onto the cell. • The cell's components reflect light in varying colors. • This allows the scientists to follow these structures when they move.
Have you ever seen shiny blue photo plankton?

media:group.media:title: Supporting reforestation in India | ZEISS
media:group.media:description:
Protecting nature means protecting our future – from clean water and air to healthy soils and biodiversity.
For ZEISS, as a foundation-owned company, sustainability and long-term business success are closely linked. Aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, our sustainability strategy focuses on three key areas: creating value for society, advancing a circular economy and driving climate action across our value chain. This includes continuously working to reduce our carbon footprint and use resources more efficiently.
In India, ZEISS has partnered to plant the ZEISS Releaf Forest close to industrial areas. The goal is to support CO₂ sequestration over time and stabilize the soil to help reduce the risk of future landslides. ZEISS contributed financial support, and our employees were also on site – planting trees side by side with our partners and bringing new life to the landscape.
This forest initiative is part of a broader commitment to conserving natural resources worldwide. In this video, you will see how our colleagues and partners turn these ideas into action – for example, by conducting soil studies in Pali, Rajasthan, selecting native species for afforestation, and creating an urban forest at the Giradha site.
You will also see how biodiversity develops and how the ecosystem is managed in a natural way, as well as how we monitor the effects on land quality and on the local community.

entry.title: How small can an electron microscope see? | ZEISS

media:group.media:title: How small can an electron microscope see? | ZEISS
media:group.media:description:
Making structures 100,000 times smaller than a human hair visible. 👀 Some details in nature are so tiny that a regular light microscope can’t resolve them. That’s where scanning electron microscopes come in. 🔬 Instead of light, they use an electron beam, which scans the surface. Watch the video to learn how this method produces an incredibly detailed image of the sample.

media:group.media:title: Selfies before smartphones | ZEISS
media:group.media:description:
Long before smartphones, taking a selfie required a lot more effort and patience. In 1839, Robert Cornelius set up his camera, opened the lens, ran into the frame, and stood completely still for over 10 minutes. ⏱️ The image was captured on a silver coated copper plate and became the first selfie in history.
Today, your phone captures moments in a fraction of a second using advanced lenses, software, and AI. It all started with one image and a lot of patience.
How long could you stay still for a selfie? 😄

entry.title: Can you see everything around you | ZEISS

media:group.media:title: Can you see everything around you | ZEISS
media:group.media:description:
Is there a way to see things that are invisible to the naked eye? 👁️ Yes, and it starts with understanding the limits of our own vision.
Your eye can only resolve details as small as the width of a human hair, roughly 80 micrometers. 💇 Anything smaller, like most cells and viruses, is simply not visible. That’s where optics come in: Microscopes make cells and life’s tiniest details visible.
If you had a microscope for one day, what’s the first thing you’d look at? 🔬

entry.title: Shaping the future with light | Photonics at ZEISS

media:group.media:title: Shaping the future with light | Photonics at ZEISS
media:group.media:description:
Light is far more than a physical phenomenon – it is a key technology driving innovation in research, medicine, industry, and our digital future with artificial intelligence. For Dr. Ulrike Böhm, physicist and R&D Scientist at ZEISS Corporate Research & Technology in Oberkochen, Germany, the fascination with light began early and never faded.
At ZEISS, photonics – the science and application of light – forms the foundation for countless technologies that shape our lives. From medical diagnostics that reveal diseases at their earliest stages, to industrial precision and quality control, to enabling the next generation of AI and quantum computing, ZEISS uses its deep understanding of light to turn fundamental physics into real‑world solutions. With expertise in optics dating back to 1846, ZEISS builds on nearly two centuries of innovation in lenses, optical systems, and photonic instruments.
Discover how Dr. Ulrike Böhm turned her childhood curiosity about light into a scientific career – and how she now works at the intersection of optics, photonics, and future technologies at ZEISS to shape the world of tomorrow: https://www.zeiss.com/photonics
00:00 Introduction Dr. Ulrike Böhm and her fascination with light 00:51 Photonics explained and its role in modern technology 01:10 Photonics as enabler in AI, robotics, healthcare, communication and mobility 02:18 How photonics shapes our understanding of the world 02:45 ZEISS legacy and what light will make possible in the future
💡 What is photonics? 💡 Photonics is the science and technology of generating, guiding, manipulating, and detecting light and other forms of radiant energy across the electromagnetic spectrum, from ultraviolet and visible to infrared. It treats light both as photons (particles) and as waves, and uses this dual nature to create high‑resolution images and reveal structures that are invisible to the naked eye, transmit and process information at extremely high speeds, measure distances, shapes, and materials with nanometer precision, and precisely modify materials, for example during micro‑ and nanofabrication.
Because of this, photonics is considered a fundamental enabling technology for the 21st century – comparable in importance to electronics and computing in the 20th. It is essential for everything from the Internet and smartphones to advanced medical diagnostics, autonomous systems, and emerging fields such as quantum technologies and next‑generation AI.

entry.title: Do fingerprints disappear when washing? | ZEISS

media:group.media:title: Do fingerprints disappear when washing? | ZEISS
media:group.media:description:
Have you ever seen what changes on a microscopic level when you wash your hands? 👀
We put fingerprints on microscope slides and compared them before and after washing.
Before washing: Clear fingerprint ridges covered with skin oils, particles, and smears; a visible protective layer naturally created by the skin.
After washing: Significantly less residue on the glass; fewer particles and a cleaner, sharper fingerprint pattern.
Our skin is constantly forming a protective surface, and hand-washing changes what stays on the things we touch. 🖐️
What should we explore next under the microscope? 🔬
